1H OurBigBook.com
Choose an integer b whose reduction is a primitive root modulo p. At least one of b,b+p satisfies gp−1≡1(modp2), because the binomial theorem gives
(b+p)p−1≡bp−1+p(p−1)bp−2(modp2),
(1)
and the added coefficient is nonzero modulo p. Both choices still generate the multiplicative group modulo p. Choose such a g and write gp−1=1+up with p∤u.
For k≥1 and p∤v, another binomial expansion shows
(1+vpk)p≡1+vpk+1(modpk+2).
(2)
The intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by p, and the final term also has valuation at least k+2 because p is odd. Induction therefore gives
vp​(g(p−1)pj−1)=j+1.
(3)
Thus gp−1 has order exactly pn−1 modulo pn. The order of g itself is divisible by p−1, by reduction modulo p, and divides the number pn−1(p−1) of invertible residue classes. Its order must consequently be precisely that number. This proves the lifting a primitive root to odd prime powers result and
(Z/pnZ)× is cyclic for every n≥1.​
(4)
For the requested example choose g=2. Modulo 11, 25≡−1 and 22≡1, excluding the proper divisors 1,2,5 of ten, so its order is ten. Also 210−1=1023=11⋅93, which is not divisible by 112. Hence
a=2 generates (Z/11nZ)× for every n≥1.​
(5)

The polynomial Runge theorem states that, for a compact set K⊂C with connected complement and a function f holomorphic on a neighborhood of K, for every ε>0 there is a polynomial P such that
z∈Ksup​∣f(z)−P(z)∣<ε.​
(6)
The connected-complement hypothesis permits polynomial approximation rather than approximation by rational functions with poles in bounded complementary components.

b OurBigBook.com
Use the Runge exhaustion of a slit disk, with the principal argument −π<argz<π:
Km​={reiθ:1/m≤r≤1−1/m,∣θ∣≤π−1/m},m≥3.
(7)
These are nested compact subsets of Ω. Their complements are connected: the inner disk and exterior region join through the omitted sector around the negative real radius. Every compact subset of Ω has positive distance from zero, the unit circle and the slit, so it is contained in Km​ for all sufficiently large m.
Since f is holomorphic on Ω, it is holomorphic on a neighborhood of each Km​. The polynomial Runge theorem gives Pm​ with supKm​​∣Pm​−f∣<1/m. Given any compact K⊂Ω, eventually K⊆Km​, so the same estimate holds on K. Therefore
Pm​⟶f uniformly on every compact subset of Ω.​
(8)
The nested exhaustion makes this one sequence work simultaneously on all compact subsets.

3G OurBigBook.com
On the unit three-ball B3, the distance in the Poincare ball model is the infimum of the lengths
L(γ)=∫1−∣γ(t)∣22∣γ′(t)∣​dt
(9)
over piecewise smooth paths joining the two points. Equivalently the hyperbolic metric as a metric-space distance is
d(x,y)=arcosh(1+(1−∣x∣2)(1−∣y∣2)2∣x−y∣2​).​
(10)
It has curvature-minus-one normalization; in particular d(0,x)=2artanh∣x∣.
For a nonempty finite set p1​,…,pm​, define R(x)=maxj​d(x,pj​). The triangle inequality gives ∣R(x)−R(y)∣≤d(x,y), so R is continuous. Take R0​=R(p1​). Any improving center satisfies d(x,p1​)≤R(x)≤R0​, and thus lies in the closed hyperbolic ball K=B(p1​,R0​).
This ball is compact: an isometry sending p1​ to the origin identifies it with the Euclidean closed ball of radius tanh(R0​/2)<1, and the Euclidean and hyperbolic topologies agree inside B3. The continuous function R attains a minimum on K. Centers outside K have R>R0​, so this is also the global minimum. Its associated closed ball proves a minimum enclosing ball in hyperbolic space exists. For the empty finite set, any center and radius zero suffice.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 217 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 217
4G OurBigBook.com
A binary cyclic code is a linear subspace of F2N​ invariant under cyclic coordinate shift. Associate a word (c0​,…,cN−1​) to ∑cj​Xj in F2​[X]/(XN−1). Cyclic shift is multiplication by X, so linearity and shift invariance make the code an ideal of this quotient.
Its inverse image in F2​[X] is an ideal containing (XN−1). Since a polynomial ring over a field is a principal ideal domain, that inverse image is (g) for a unique monic polynomial g. Containment gives XN−1=gh for some polynomial h. Thus the generator polynomial of a cyclic code satisfies
g∣XN−1,C=(g) modulo XN−1.​
(11)
For a nonzero code g is also its monic word polynomial of smallest degree. For the zero code use g=XN−1, whose residue is zero. Conversely every monic divisor defines a cyclic code, proving the full correspondence.
Over F2​,
X5−1=(X+1)(X4+X3+X2+X+1).
(12)
The quartic factor has no root in F2​. The only monic irreducible quadratic over this field is X2+X+1, and division leaves remainder X+1, so the quartic is not divisible by it. A reducible quartic with no linear factor would have two irreducible quadratic factors; hence this quartic is irreducible. There are exactly four binary cyclic codes of length five, given by the generator polynomials of a cyclic code
1,X+1,X4+X3+X2+X+1,X5−1.​
(13)
They are respectively the full space, the even-weight code, the repetition code and the zero code, with dimensions 5,4,1,0.

5J OurBigBook.com
These are nested Poisson regression models with independent counts and the default log link function. If xi​ is biomass and gi​ is the three-level pH group, model 1 specifies logμi​=α+βxi​: one common intercept and slope. Model 2 specifies logμi​=αgi​​+βxi​: three group-specific intercepts and a common slope. Model 3 specifies logμi​=αgi​​+βgi​​xi​: three intercepts and three slopes, because the multiplication syntax includes both main effects and their interaction. The parameter counts are therefore 2,4,6.
The analysis of deviance compares model 1 against model 2 by testing equality of the three intercepts, conditional on a common biomass slope. The likelihood-ratio test statistic is 407.67−99.24=308.43 with two additional parameters, giving the reported tiny p-value. The next test compares model 2 against model 3 by testing equality of their three slopes. Its statistic is 99.24−83.20=16.04, again with two degrees of freedom and reported p=3.288×10−4. Both restrictions are rejected. Thus model 3 is the supported choice: both baseline richness and its biomass dependence vary with pH. Under the Poisson assumptions, residual deviance 83.20 on 84 residual degrees of freedom is also consistent with a satisfactory fit, although these nested tests themselves establish improvement rather than every possible aspect of model adequacy.
The prediction from model 2 is on its linear-predictor scale. Exponentiating gives its fitted means. The final expression is twice the saturated log likelihood minus the model-2 log likelihood, i.e. the Poisson deviance of model 2. Consequently
The returned value is 99.24, up to the table’s rounding.​
(14)
In the saturated model each mean equals the corresponding observed count, with the usual continuous convention for a zero count.

6B OurBigBook.com
Balancing the viscous and bending terms gives ζωh∼Ah/ℓ4, so the elastohydrodynamic penetration length is
ℓ=(A/(ζω))1/4.​
(15)
Inserting h=h0​Re[eiωtF(x/ℓ)] into the linear equation yields F′′′′=−iF, with F(0)=1, F′′(0)=0 and decay at infinity. Write C=cos(π/8), S=sin(π/8). Of the four roots of λ4=−i, precisely two have negative real part:
λL​=−C+iS,λR​=−S−iC.
(16)
The two decaying solutions are eλL​η and eλR​η, and the general decaying response is their linear combination. Both coefficients are nonzero: if one vanished, F′′(0)=0 would force the other to vanish, contradicting F(0)=1.
Their real parts in the time-dependent response are proportional to
e−Cηcos(ωt+Sη+ϕL​),e−Sηcos(ωt−Cη+ϕR​).
(17)
Constant phases move respectively with velocities −ωℓ/S and ωℓ/C, so these are damped travelling waves moving left and right. Since S<C, the right-going wave has the longer attenuation length and dominates at large x. Thus the less strongly damped, outward-moving wave dominates the far-field response. This is the oscillatory bending of a moment-free semi-infinite filament; the two boundary conditions determine its amplitudes without needing them explicitly here.

Words: 193
7A OurBigBook.com
In Glendinning chaos, a continuous interval map is chaotic when some positive iterate has a horseshoe for an interval map. In the interval version, one may take an open interval J containing two disjoint open intervals K0​,K1​ with Fm(K0​)=Fm(K1​)=J.
Let a three-cycle be ordered a<b<c. There are only two possible cyclic orderings; reflection of the coordinate interchanges them, so assume F(a)=b, F(b)=c, F(c)=a. Then
F2(a)=c,F2(b)=a.
(18)
Also F(b)=c and F(c)=a, so the intermediate value theorem gives d∈(b,c) with F(d)=b, whence F2(d)=c. Both [a,b] and [b,d] therefore map across [a,c] under F2.
To obtain exact open-interval images, use the following elementary first-passage observation. A continuous function on [r,s] with endpoint values a,c has a subinterval on which its endpoint values are a,c and all interior values lie strictly between them: take the first hit of the second level, then the last hit of the first level before it. The intermediate value theorem makes its interior image exactly (a,c). Apply this to the two intervals, reversing endpoint order on the first. Their selected interiors K0​⊂(a,b) and K1​⊂(b,d) are disjoint and lie in J=(a,c), with
F2(K0​)=F2(K1​)=J.​
(19)
This proves the three-cycle forces a two-iterate interval horseshoe result and establishes the required horseshoe for F2.

For real t, indent the upper-half-plane contour above the pole of G(z)/(z−t). The clockwise indentation contributes −iπG(t), while the large semicircle contributes zero in the limit. The Cauchy integral theorem gives
PV∫−∞∞​τ−tG(τ)​dτ=iπG(t).
(20)
With the stated Hilbert transform convention this is HG(t)=−iG(t). But
G(t)=tsint​+it1−cost​.
(21)
Taking real parts yields the Hilbert transform of the sinc function:
H(tsint​)=t1−cost​.​
(22)
At t=0 the right side has limit zero; the same value follows by oddness of the principal-value integrand. The apparent singularity of G at zero is removable, so the contour calculation is valid there too.

10E OurBigBook.com
With a prime denoting conformal-time differentiation, a′=aa˙ and H=a′/a=a˙. Multiplying the Friedmann equation by a2 gives H2+kc2=8πGρa2/3, and hence
kc2/H2=Ω−1.​
(27)
The Friedmann acceleration equation and P=wρc2 give
H′=aa¨=−34πG​ρa2(1+3w)=−21+3w​(H2+kc2).
(28)
Differentiate Ω−1=kc2/H2 and substitute this expression:
Ω′=(1+3w)HΩ(Ω−1).​
(29)
For k=0, Ω=1 identically and the same equation holds directly. The relations assume H=0, as is true on the expanding branch in the question.
For pressureless matter, w=0, the cosmological density parameter flow points away from Ω=1: initial Ω>1 increases, while 0<Ω<1 decreases. In the closed case the expanding branch can end at a turnaround, where H=0 and this density parameter diverges. For vacuum domination, w=−1, the sign reverses: values above one decrease and positive values below one increase toward one. The plotted curves are representative conformal-time solutions with c=1 and separately chosen origins; inflationary future infinity occurs at a finite conformal time.
In a decelerating matter or radiation era, small deviations from flatness grow: near one, dlog∣Ω−1∣/dloga≃1+3w>0. Observed near-flatness therefore requires extremely small earlier deviations, the flatness problem. During accelerated expansion with w<−1/3, this exponent is negative and curvature is driven toward negligible relative size. For w=−1, ∣Ω−1∣ decays approximately as a−2. Sufficiently long cosmic inflation supplies the inflationary solution of the flatness problem before ordinary decelerating evolution resumes.

Put α=N​ and use conventional convergent indexing starting at zero; the same argument covers all the printed positive indices. The continued fraction complete quotients satisfy αj+1​=1/(αj​−aj​), aj​=⌊αj​⌋. After the first step they exceed one, while their algebraic conjugates lie in (−1,0). Indeed α1′​=1/(−N​−a0​)∈(−1,0), and if αj′​∈(−1,0) with aj​≥1, then 1/(αj′​−aj​)∈(−1,0).
Write αk+1​=(N​+m)/d, where m,d are integers and d>0. This form follows by rationalization at each step: mj+1​=aj​dj​−mj​ and dj+1​=(N−mj+12​)/dj​, starting from m0​=0,d0​=1. The two conjugate inequalities give
d<N​+m,m<N​,
(30)
so d<2N​. The standard convergent recursions also give
N​=qk​αk+1​+qk−1​pk​αk+1​+pk−1​​,∣pk​qk−1​−qk​pk−1​∣=1.
(31)
Substitute the displayed form of αk+1​ and compare rational and irrational coefficients. This yields pk​=mqk​+dqk−1​ and Nqk​=mpk​+dpk−1​. Therefore the small norm residues from square-root continued fractions obey
pk2​−Nqk2​=d(pk​qk−1​−qk​pk−1​),∣pk2​−Nqk2​∣=d<2N​.​
(32)
The initial convergent satisfies the same relation with the usual p−1​=1,q−1​=0. This avoids the insufficient estimate obtained by merely replacing the convergent error with 1/qk2​.
For integer factorization, choose a factor base of small primes for which N is a quadratic residue, together with −1 to record negative residues; a prime dividing N already supplies a factor. Test the small nonzero integers rk​=pk2​−Nqk2​ for being B-numbers. Complete factorization over the base records each prime exponent modulo two. Once enough relations are collected, linear algebra over F2​ can choose a nonempty subcollection whose exponent sum is even, including the sign. Then
∏rk​=Y2,X=∏pk​,X2≡Y2(modN).
(33)
If X≡±Y(modN), one of gcd(X−Y,N) or gcd(X+Y,N) can yield a nontrivial factor. Relations with a noninvertible pk​ may already give a factor through its gcd. The small-residue bound makes smoothness more likely; it does not guarantee that any one dependency gives a nontrivial factor.

Words: 201 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 201
12G OurBigBook.com
A subgroup of the Möbius group PSL2​(C) is a discrete subgroup when the identity is isolated in its induced topology, equivalently every group element is isolated. We prove the compact-set criterion for a properly discontinuous group action: for every compact K⊂H3, only finitely many g∈G satisfy gK∩K=∅.
Fix an origin o and take K⊆B(o,R). If x∈K and gx∈K, the triangle inequality and invariance of hyperbolic distance give
d(o,go)≤d(o,gx)+d(gx,go)=d(o,gx)+d(x,o)≤2R.
(34)
The set of Möbius isometries with d(o,go)≤2R is compact. To see this explicitly, represent an isometry by a determinant-one complex matrix and use singular-value decomposition:
g=k1​(es/20​0e−s/2​)k2​,k1​,k2​∈SU(2),s≥0.
(35)
The compact factors fix o, and the diagonal factor moves it hyperbolic distance s, as seen from the vertical dilation by es in upper half-space. Thus the bounded-displacement set is the continuous image of SU(2)×[0,2R]×SU(2), modulo central signs.
By the allowed closedness fact, its intersection with G is a closed discrete subset of a compact space, hence finite. Otherwise an infinite sequence would accumulate in that intersection, contradicting isolation of its limit point. This proves every discrete Möbius subgroup acts properly discontinuously on hyperbolic three-space. Finite stabilizers are allowed; discreteness alone does not imply a free action.

Write θi​=θ(μi​) and ηi​=xiT​β=g(μi​). Differentiating μi​=K′(θi​) gives dμi​/dθi​=V(μi​), so
∂βj​∂θi​​=V(μi​)g′(μi​)xij​​.
(36)
In the independent exponential dispersion family, only [yi​θi​−K(θi​)]/σi2​ depends on β. Its derivative therefore gives the score function
Uj​=i∑​σi2​V(μi​)g′(μi​)(yi​−μi​)xij​​.​
(37)
The residuals are independent, have mean zero and variance σi2​V(μi​). Consequently their score covariance is the Fisher information matrix:
Ijk​=E(Uj​Uk​)=i∑​σi2​V(μi​)[g′(μi​)]2xij​xik​​.​
(38)
This also equals minus the expected likelihood Hessian under the usual regularity conditions.
For the canonical link function, g(μ)=θ(μ) and g′=1/V, so
Uj​=i∑​σi2​(yi​−μi​)xij​​,Ijk​=i∑​σi2​V(μi​)xij​xik​​.​
(39)
To obtain the maximum-likelihood estimate, solve U(β​)=0, for example with Fisher scoring iterations βnew=β+I(β)−1U(β). Equivalently use iteratively reweighted least squares, with weights [σi2​V(μi​)g′(μi​)2]−1 and working response ηi​+(yi​−μi​)g′(μi​). Since σi2​=σ2ai​, the common dispersion scale cancels from this update for β. A nonsingular information matrix and a finite interior likelihood maximum are needed; iteration does not assert those for every possible dataset.

For a flow, a hyperbolic fixed point has no eigenvalue of its linearization with zero real part; a nonhyperbolic fixed point has at least one such eigenvalue. At (μ,0) the eigenvalues are −μ,1−μ, while at (0,±1) they are μ+1,−2. Thus nonhyperbolicity occurs at the two stated parameters. The following centre manifold reductions show the associated actual bifurcations.
Near (1,0) put X=x−μ, Y=y, ν=μ−1. The transformed equations are
X˙=(1+ν+X)(−X+Y2),Y˙=Y(−ν−X−Y2),ν˙=0.
(40)
At ν=0, the non-extended stable subspace is the X axis and the centre subspace is the Y axis. In the extended centre manifold, write X=h(Y,ν), with h(0,ν)=0. The symmetry Y↦−Y allows an even graph. At quadratic order its invariance equation has left side of degree at least three and right side −h+Y2, so h=Y2+O(νY2,Y4). Substitution gives
Y˙=−νY−2Y3+O(νY3,Y5).​
(41)
This is a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation in parameter −ν=1−μ. The central branch is stable for μ>1 and unstable for μ<1 near one; the two nonzero branches for μ<1 are stable. At the bifurcation itself the cubic term attracts on the centre manifold.
Near (0,1) put X=x, Y=y−1, ν=μ+1. Then
X˙=X(ν−X+2Y+Y2),Y˙=(1+Y)(−X−2Y−Y2),ν˙=0.
(42)
At ν=0, the stable subspace is X=0 and the centre line is Y=−X/2. Thus the leading extended centre graph is Y=−X/2+O(X2,νX), and the reduced flow is
X˙=νX−2X2+O(X3,νX2).​
(43)
This is a transcritical bifurcation: X=0 is stable for ν<0, while the branch X=ν/2+⋯ is stable for ν>0; the opposite branches are unstable. At the critical point the quadratic term is only one-sided attracting.
The exact additional branch in y>0 is
x=(μ+1)/2,y=(1−μ)/2​,μ<1.​
(44)
It meets (μ,0) at μ=1 and (0,1) at μ=−1, displaying the connecting pitchfork and transcritical branches in a quadratic-product flow. Its Jacobian has determinant 1−μ2 and trace (μ−3)/2. Hence it is stable for −1<μ<1 and a saddle for μ<−1. The negative-y companion is needed for the pitchfork sketch near (1,0); no separate analysis of (0,−1) is required.

For a regular periodic energy orbit, differentiate the action integral with respect to its energy. On a branch H(p,q)=E, implicit differentiation gives ∂p/∂E=1/Hp​=1/q˙​. Thus
dEdI​=2π1​∮q˙​dq​=2πT​,dIdH​=T2π​.​
(47)
The integral follows the entire orbit, with its orientation; at turning points this formula is interpreted by the limiting integral from each branch. It is valid for a smooth family of nonseparatrix periodic orbits.
An adiabatic invariant means that the action variable remains constant to leading order when the external parameter changes on a timescale much longer than the orbital period. Denote that parameter by λ. With H(0,λ)=0, the displayed identity integrates to
H(I,λ)=∫0I​T(J,λ)2π​dJ.
(48)
If the parameter change decreases T(J,λ) for every intervening action J, this integrand increases pointwise. At the adiabatically fixed positive I, the energy increases. This uses the phrase “with any I” as a statement about the family of orbits, not merely a period decrease at a single selected action; that weaker premise alone would not determine the integral.

Solution

16G OurBigBook.com
For Hartogs theorem, collect all well-order relations on all subsets of a set x. They form a set, since the relations belong to the power set of x×x. Replacement collects their ordinal order types in a set T. Define
α=sup{β+1:β∈T}.
(49)
If there were an injection α→x, transfer the well-order of α to its image. Its type would put α in T, giving α+1≤α, impossible. Thus some ordinal does not inject into x, without using choice.
Assume the axiom of choice and let a nonempty partially ordered set P have an upper bound for every chain. Suppose it has no maximal element. Choose, from every subset of P with a nonempty set of strict upper bounds, one such strict upper bound. Every chain has a strict upper bound: first take an upper bound and then a strictly larger element, using the absence of maximal elements. Take a Hartogs ordinal α for P. Transfinite recursion chooses pβ​, for each β<α, strictly above all previously chosen elements. Their predecessors form a chain at every stage, so this recursion is defined and strictly increasing. It gives an injection α→P, contradicting the choice of α. Hence P has a maximal element, proving Zorn's lemma.
For the well-ordering theorem, take a choice function on the nonempty subsets of x and recursively choose an element of x not previously selected. If this process had not exhausted x at any stage below its Hartogs ordinal α, it would define an injection α→x, again impossible. Therefore it exhausts x at some ordinal stage β<α. Order each element by its unique selection index; this transfers the ordinal well-order to all of x. The empty set is already well-ordered. These proofs use transfinite recursion, not an unstated fixed-point theorem.

Define the multicolour graph Ramsey number Rk​(s1​,…,sk​) as the least n such that every colouring of the edges of the complete graph Kn​ with k colours contains, for some i, a complete subgraph on si​ vertices all of whose edges have colour i.
Prove finiteness by induction on ∑i​si​, temporarily allowing si​=1. If some si​=1, a single vertex supplies the required vacuous monochromatic clique, so the Ramsey number is one. Otherwise put Ni​=Rk​(s1​,…,si​−1,…,sk​), which is finite by induction, and take
n=∑i​Ni​−k+2.
(50)
Fix a vertex v and partition its other n−1 vertices according to the colour of their edge to v. Some colour-i class has at least Ni​ vertices: if every class had at most Ni​−1, their total would be at most ∑i​Ni​−k=n−2. In that class the inductive property either gives a colour-j clique of size sj​ with j=i, or a colour-i clique of size si​−1. In the latter case add v. Thus
Rk​(s1​,…,sk​)≤i∑​Rk​(s1​,…,si​−1,…,sk​)−k+2<∞.​
(51)
In particular the requested two-colour diagonal number is R(s)=R2​(s,s), so it exists for every s≥2.
Now colour each positive integer by its partition class, say there are k classes, and take m=Rk​(3,…,3). Colour the edge ij, 1≤i<j≤m, by the class of j−i. There is a monochromatic triangle a<b<c. Its three differences x=b−a, y=c−b, z=c−a are positive integers in one class, and
x+y=z.​
(52)
This is the finite-Ramsey proof of the partition conclusion. The statement does not require x and y to be distinct.

For odd prime n, every subgroup is one of {1}, ⟨σ⟩, a reflection subgroup Hj​=⟨σjτ⟩ for 0≤j<n, or G. Indeed, a subgroup containing a nonidentity rotation contains all rotations; with any reflection it is then G. A subgroup with no nonidentity rotation contains at most one reflection, since the product of distinct reflections is a nonidentity rotation.
The Galois correspondence gives the following fixed fields. The trivial subgroup corresponds to L=C(z), the rotation subgroup to C(zn), and G to the base C(w). Since composition of the stated automorphisms gives (σjτ)(z)=ζn−j​/z, the reflection subgroup corresponds to
LHj​=C(z+ζn−j​/z).​
(55)
This rational invariant has degree two, hence generates the fixed field of its order-two subgroup, by the same degree argument as part (i). These fields have degrees respectively 2n,2,n,1 over C(w).
An intermediate field is Galois over the base exactly when its corresponding subgroup is normal in G. The trivial subgroup, the rotations and G are normal; no reflection subgroup is normal because n is odd and greater than two. Hence the Galois intermediate extensions and groups are
Gal(L/C(w))=G,Gal(C(zn)/C(w))≅C2​,Gal(C(w)/C(w))={1}.​
(56)
The n reflection fixed fields are not Galois over the base.

Work over the complex numbers. By Maschke's theorem, restriction to the normal subgroup A is a direct sum of its isotypic components. For an irreducible A-type W, denote its isotypic component in V by VW​. Normality makes G permute these components, by conjugating the A-types. Any union of orbits spans a G-invariant subspace, so irreducibility of V means that all occurring components form a single orbit.
If there is only one component, restriction is isotypic, as claimed. Otherwise take one component VW​ and its stabilizer H={g:gVW​=VW​}, a proper subgroup. This is an irreducible representation of H: if 0=U⊊VW​ were H-invariant, the direct sum of its translates over coset representatives for G/H would be a nonzero proper G-invariant subspace of V. It is direct because the translates lie in distinct isotypic components, and proper because dimU<dimVW​.
The natural map from the induced representation sends g⊗v to gv. It identifies the direct-sum coset decomposition with all isotypic components of V, so is bijective and G-equivariant. Consequently
V≅IndHG​VW​.​
(57)
This proves the dichotomy directly, including the irreducibility of the representation being induced.

Induct on the order of the p-group. Every complex irreducible representation of an abelian group is one-dimensional: commuting group operators preserve a common eigenspace, and irreducibility makes that eigenspace the whole space. This handles the abelian cases.
If V is not faithful, it is an irreducible representation of a smaller quotient G/K, where K is its kernel. Induction expresses it as induced from a one-dimensional representation of a subgroup of G/K. Pulling back the subgroup and inflating the character gives the same induction statement for G, because the coset spaces of the quotient subgroup and its inverse image agree.
Now suppose V is faithful and G is nonabelian. Use the allowed abelian normal subgroup A not contained in the centre. If restriction to A were isotypic, its irreducible type would be one-dimensional, so every a∈A would act as a scalar. It would therefore commute with every representing matrix of G. Faithfulness would imply ga=ag in G for every g, contradicting the choice of A. By part (a), V=IndHG​W for an irreducible representation of a proper subgroup H. Induction on H gives W=IndKH​χ with χ one-dimensional. Transitivity of induction yields
V=IndKG​χ.​
(58)
This proves the monomiality of irreducible representations of finite p-groups.

For k=Q(2​), the standard quadratic-integer criterion gives Ok​=Z[2​], since 2 is squarefree and is not congruent to one modulo four. Thus
1,2​ is an integral basis of k.​

TrK/k​θ=2a+2c2​,TrK/k​(αθ)=4d+2b2​.
(60)
Both are in Ok​, proving 2a,2b,2c,4d∈Z. Multiplying θ by its conjugate gives the field norm
NK/k​θ=(a+c2​)2−2​(b+d2​)2=(a2+2c2−4bd)+(2ac−b2−2d2)2​.

Again this is in Ok​, so both displayed coefficients are integers.
To finish the denominator argument, put A=2a, B=2b, C=2c, D=4d, all integers. The two norm coefficients imply
A2+2C2−2BD≡0(mod4),4AC−2B2−D2≡0(mod8).
(62)
The second congruence modulo two first gives D even. Modulo four it then gives B even. Therefore 2BD vanishes modulo four, and the first congruence reads A2+2C2≡0(mod4). The possible squares modulo four force A even and then C even. Returning to the second congruence now gives D2≡0(mod8), so D is divisible by four. Thus a,b,c,d are all integers.
Conversely, every integer linear combination of these powers is integral. We have proved the integral basis of the fourth-root-of-two field:
OK​=Z[α],1,α,α2,α3 is an integral basis.​

Since the covering spaces are simply connected, the path lifting theorem constructs lifts f​ of fpX​ and g​ of gpY​, after specifying one value in the appropriate fiber. Explicitly, define the lift at a point by lifting the image of a path from the chosen base point; independence from the path follows from simple connectedness and homotopy lifting.

Such a lift of the identity is a deck transformation and is a homeomorphism: lift the identity again with the base point image reversed, and uniqueness of path lifts makes the two compositions identities. The function z↦℘(−z) has the same periodicity, poles and normalized Laurent behavior as ℘(z). Uniqueness in its definition therefore makes ℘ even, so ℘′ is odd. At a nonzero half-period b with 2b∈Λ, periodicity and oddness give ℘′(b)=℘′(−b)=−℘′(b), hence zero. Modulo Λ the three such points are 1/2, τ/2, (1+τ)/2.
An elliptic function has equal total orders of zeros and poles in a period cell, by the argument principle and cancellation of opposite boundary edges. The derivative has exactly one pole modulo the lattice, of order three at zero. The three displayed zeros therefore exhaust its zeros, each with multiplicity one:
℘′(z)=0⟺z≡1/2,τ/2,(1+τ)/2(modΛ).​
(74)
The only potential poles of h outside the lattice are at z=a and z=−a. Since 2a∈/Λ, these points are distinct modulo the lattice and ℘′(a)=0. At each point the squared factor (℘(z)−℘(a))2 vanishes to order two, canceling the double pole of the shifted Weierstrass elliptic function. The derivative term is regular there. Thus h has no poles outside Λ.
Near zero write ℘(z)=z−2+c2​z2+O(z4), using evenness and the normalization. Taylor expansion at a gives
℘(z−a)−℘(z+a)=−2℘′(a)z−31​℘′′′(a)z3+O(z5).
(75)
Consequently
h(z)=[4℘(a)℘′(a)−31​℘′′′(a)]z−1+O(z).
(76)
The z−3 terms cancel exactly, and there are no z−2 terms. Thus there is at most one simple pole per period cell. The sum of residues of an elliptic function over a period cell is zero, again because opposite boundary contour integrals cancel; its sole possible residue must vanish. Hence h is entire. Periodicity makes it bounded on the plane, and Liouville's theorem makes it constant. In fact h is odd, so that constant is zero. The resulting Weierstrass shift-difference identity by pole cancellation is
h≡0.​
(77)

A sufficient statistic T has a conditional distribution of the data given T that does not depend on the parameter. In a dominated family, the factorization criterion for sufficiency states that this is equivalent to pμ​(x)=h(x)gμ​(T(x)) for a nonnegative parameter-free h. Bayes' formula then gives a posterior distribution proportional to π(μ)gμ​(T(x)), because h(x) cancels from numerator and normalizing denominator. Thus the posterior depends on the data only through T.
For the normal sample,
∑i​(xi​−μ)2=∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2+n(xˉ−μ)2.
(97)
The first term is parameter-free, so the factorization proves sufficiency of Xˉ. Combining its likelihood with the normal prior and completing the square gives
M∣X1​,…,Xn​∼N(1+nτ2nτ2​xˉ,1+nτ2τ2​).​
(98)
The prior predictive distribution of the sample mean is obtained from Xˉ=M+ε, ε∼N(0,1/n) independent of M:
Xˉ∼N(0,τ2+1/n).​
(99)
Define the Bayes factor B01​ as the marginal likelihood under H0​ divided by that under H1​. The common residual factor cancels, so it is the ratio of the densities of Xˉ under these two hypotheses:
B01​=1+nτ2​exp[−2(1+nτ2)n2τ2xˉ2​].​
(100)
The reverse Bayes factor is its reciprocal. At ∣xˉ∣=1.96/n​,
B01​=1+nτ2​exp[−21.962​1+nτ2nτ2​]∼τn​e−1.962/2⟶∞
(101)
for a fixed positive τ. Thus the frequentist test is at its rejection threshold while fixed prior odds give increasingly strong posterior support for the point null. This is the Jeffreys-Lindley paradox for a Gaussian point null: the standardized statistic stays fixed, but the observed effect tends to zero and the fixed-scale alternative spreads predictive mass much more widely. There is no logical contradiction, since the procedures compare hypotheses using different calibrations. For the degenerate τ=0 the hypotheses coincide and B01​=1.

The optimal control maximizes H, the costate obeys ψ˙​=−Hx​, and free terminal time at the fixed terminal state zero gives H(τ)=λ0​C′(τ). Maximization gives full power for p(t)<p∗​ and zero power for p(t)>p∗​; either value, or a fractional value, is allowed on a price tie. On the final active arc, the free-time condition gives
p∗​+R′(τ∗​)=p(τ∗​).​

For p∗​=1/4, processing starts at t=1/2. Energy 1/2 is completed at τ=1, before the price rises again. Its cost and reward are

At a fixed τ∈[1/2,5/4], the cheapest half-unit of processing consists of the last half-unit interval [τ−1/2,τ]: every earlier point has a price at least as large as every selected point. Exchanging any earlier powered interval with a later unpowered cheaper one proves this rearrangement claim, also for fractional controls.

33E (Applications of Quantum Mechanics)

Words: 264 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 264
33E OurBigBook.com
A periodic lattice Hamiltonian commutes with lattice translations. The Bloch theorem therefore classifies its states by characters of the translation group:
ψnk​(x)=eik⋅xunk​(x),
(127)
where u is lattice periodic. For each crystal momentum k, solving on a primitive cell with the corresponding quasiperiodic boundary condition gives discrete eigenvalues indexed by n. Their continuous dependence on k produces the energy bands En​(k) as k ranges through the Brillouin zone. Bragg mixing opens gaps at suitable degeneracies, although bands can overlap in three dimensions and gaps are not guaranteed between every pair.
The quantum numbers are band index, wavevector modulo reciprocal lattice vectors, and spin where spin is conserved. In a finite crystal the allowed wavevectors are discrete; in the thermodynamic limit they become dense and the band description emerges. Spin-orbit coupling can replace a separately conserved spin label by an appropriate internal band label.
Dilute randomly placed impurities break exact translation symmetry, so crystal momentum is no longer an exact quantum number. Most extended states retain approximately the host band structure but acquire impurity scattering and disorder broadening. An impurity potential can also produce impurity levels in a crystal, often in a band gap: levels associated with a donor impurity lie near the conduction-band edge and can supply electrons, while those associated with an acceptor impurity lie near the valence-band edge and can create holes. The impurity's species and potential determine whether such levels exist and how deep they are; not every impurity necessarily makes a gap state. At low density these levels are nearly isolated, while overlap at increasing density can broaden them into an impurity band. Added or removed carriers shift the chemical potential as well.

Using the given fourth-power integral in the normalization gives 1=4k4[4/(3k)]=16k3/3, so k=(3/16)1/3. Thus the similarity profile of an axisymmetric radial viscous free jet is
ur​(r,z)=r(9F2/(32ν))1/3​sech2[(3F/(16ν2))1/3rz​].​
(151)
It is symmetric, outward, decays in z, and has exactly the conserved flux F. It describes the region beyond the small injection slit where the stated boundary-layer approximation applies; its formal r=0 singularity is outside that approximation.

Take a horizontally polarized shear displacement u(y)ei(kx−ωt), with k>0 and c=ω/k. In the layer put q=c2/cˉs2​−1​ and in the half-space put γ=1−c2/cs2​​. The required inequality makes both positive. The shear-wave equations give
ulayer​=Acos[kq(y−h)],uhalf​=Bekγy,
(152)
where the first form satisfies zero traction at y=h and the second decays as y→−∞. Displacement and traction continuity at zero give Acos(kqh)=B and μˉ​kqAsin(kqh)=μkγB. Hence the Love wave dispersion relation is
tan(khq)=μˉ​qμγ​.​
(153)
The left-hand square root uses the layer speed cˉs​, as in the original PDF; the TeX aid incorrectly omits its bar there.
Let K=kh>0 and qmax​=cs2​/cˉs2​−1​. The allowed interval is 0<q<qmax​, and the right side becomes
μˉ​μ​cs​cˉs​​qqmax2​−q2​​,
(154)
a positive strictly decreasing function from infinity to zero. On each positive branch of tan(Kq) beginning at Kq=mπ, the left side is strictly increasing from zero to infinity, or to a positive endpoint value if qmax​ comes first. There is exactly one intersection on that branch whenever mπ<Kqmax​. The fundamental branch m=0 thus supplies a real solution for every positive kh.
The second branch exists precisely when Kqmax​>π. Thus the strict cutoff of the second Love-wave mode is
(kh)cutoff​=cs2​/cˉs2​−1​π​,two trapped modes iff kh>(kh)cutoff​.​
(155)
At equality the second solution would have c=cs​, zero half-space decay exponent, and fails the required disturbance decay. Consequently the cutoff is the infimum, rather than an attained smallest value, under the printed strict speed inequality. Also kh=0 itself is a limiting case, not a trapped propagating mode; the “any value” assertion is valid for positive kh.

a OurBigBook.com
Since A is diagonalizable over the complex numbers, write x(0)=∑i​ai​vi​. Provided iteration does not encounter zero, its direction is that of
Akx(0)=∑i​ai​λik​vi​.
(156)
With one strictly dominant eigenvalue and an​=0, all other contributions are smaller by factors (∣λi​∣/∣λn​∣)k. The dominant eigenvalue is real, since nonreal eigenvalues of a real matrix occur in conjugate pairs of equal modulus. The normalized power method therefore converges to a signed unit eigenvector if λn​>0, and alternates between opposite unit eigenvectors if λn​<0. A quotient such as (x(k))TAx(k) approaches λn​ in either case. If an​=0, replace it by the largest active modulus; if Ax(k)=0, the prescribed iteration is undefined.
With two dominant eigenvalues of equal modulus and both components active, the iterates approach their real invariant plane rather than one direction. Distinct real equal-modulus eigenvalues are ρ,−ρ and produce a limiting two-cycle. A conjugate pair ρe±iθ produces a rotation in suitable coordinates on that plane: the normalized directions are periodic when the angle is rational relative to 2π and otherwise generally keep rotating without convergence. If the two eigenvalues are equal and real, the initial projection is itself one eigenvector in their repeated eigenspace, and converges or alternates as in the single-value case; one orbit cannot recover every independent eigenvector of that eigenspace.
For distinct dominant values, retain unnormalized consecutive vectors y,Ay,A2y in the nearly invariant plane and solve
A2y=sAy−py.
(157)
The roots of λ2−sλ+p estimate the two eigenvalues. Corresponding eigenvectors are Ay−λ2​y and Ay−λ1​y, since applying A and using the recurrence multiplies them by λ1​ and λ2​. This is dominant eigenpair extraction from a two-step Krylov recurrence. Equivalent extraction uses the 2×2 matrix of A on the computed plane. It needs two independent iterates and nonzero projections onto both distinct eigenvectors.

The given vectors satisfy
yk+2​=2yk+1​−2yk​,
(158)
and yk​,yk+1​ are independent, so their span is invariant under A. On that plane the characteristic polynomial is λ2−2λ+2. Therefore
λ±​=1±i,v±​=yk+1​−(1∓i)yk​=(1±i,2±i,3±i)T.​
(159)
Indeed Av±​=yk+2​−(1∓i)yk+1​=(1±i)v±​. No third eigenvalue is determined by these data.
The displayed xk​=(1,1,1) has norm 3​, although a large-k normalized iterate should have norm one. This harmless source normalization is resolved by dividing all three displayed vectors by 3​; the recurrence, eigenvalues and eigenvector directions are unchanged.
